analysis.title: GS flow and positioning observations
key_insights: US equities liquidated sharply on 11/5 (the day the note describes): Nasdaq -5.5% by the EMEA desk's early read, SOX -12%, SPX -4.4%. The US desk's close shows NDX -6.36% (worst day since 3/9/2020), S&P -4.36% to 7,353, R2K -4.46%, Dow -3.44%. Day one after the election saw AI underperform while the broader market rallied on a perceived pivot to the political center. Day two was a violent catch-down.

The EMEA desk (Privorotsky) says mechanical selling compounded the drop: leveraged ETF rebalancing in semis and NDX, with selling into the close, plus negative dealer gamma. He calls it a self-reinforcing liquidation. VVIX had its largest one-day move since Volmageddon (Feb 5, 2018).

The cash franchise net sold -$3bn in the US, with Tech (Info Tech + Comm Services) -$2.2bn of it. The Tech unwind since it began totals -$27bn, larger than the July technical unwind's -$21bn. GS AIS says semis pressure reflects absent underlying demand, particularly from long-only funds. Multi-strat, quant, long-only and retail are all moving in the same direction.

Privorotsky frames the question as 1998 versus March 2000 and leans toward 1998. In 1998 the shock was external and US growth stayed intact, and markets recovered once liquidity returned and the Fed eased. He argues today's AI leaders have real revenues, cash flows and balance sheets, and that delayed data centers do not destroy compute demand. He flags the 2000 parallel as the scale of spending and uncertainty around returns.

Privorotsky lists four AI concerns: insufficient capital to finance the buildout, insufficient revenue to justify investment, insufficient power and permitting capacity, and an unsustainable aggregate spending trajectory. He says the market has latched onto power and permitting, which he calls arguably the least important. The real question is whether revenues justify the capital employed.

Politics: Privorotsky reads Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's comments on data centers as a regulatory reset rather than ideological rejection. He thinks actual spending could surprise positively versus what the market is now discounting.

Energy: oil rebounded about 4% on the prior day and was higher again that morning, as markets had priced an immediate Iran off-ramp too early. Negotiations are unresolved, with renewed escalation a risk. Privorotsky says it is hard to see the broader tape perform without more confidence on energy. WTI closed +2.80% at $90.58.

Technical and risk read: Nasdaq has broken its 200-day moving average and the S&P sits just above it, which Privorotsky says needs to hold. Negative gamma leaves room for violent moves both ways. He thinks the de-rating is justified by fundamental uncertainty but the last leg is overextended, and names higher-quality tech such as TSMC and ASML. He expects defense into the weekend. He cites the S&P being higher 12 months after each of the 19 midterms since 1950, stressing this is a 12-month observation, not a one-month forecast.
What changes the narrative, per Privorotsky: political reflexivity around AI investment and growth, stabilization in funding markets, and evidence that spending and demand remain intact.

US sales trading (Contessa/Callahan): the selloff centered on semis and AI adjacencies as the market recalibrates data center gigawatt build forecasts. Moves were most evident in engineering and construction names for data centers, independent power producers and power, neoclouds, and semiconductors. SOX multiples have compressed about 50% from the June/July highs. The next debate is whether downside to gigawatt and capex outlooks is now overpriced.

US activity and flows: asset managers finished net sellers on steady supply across semis and AI. The desk saw no offsetting bid for hyperscalers or defensive tech, which had supported the index the day before. Hedge fund flows were roughly balanced while aggressively toggling short books. ETFs were 32% of volume, the largest share since June. High beta momentum fell 6.2% and is 51% off its June highs, the worst drawdown in over 10 years. Many AI-related baskets had their biggest down day since ChatGPT launched.

CTA positioning: futures closed below the medium-term CTA threshold at 7,549. The desk expects incremental US supply, with a -2.5 standard deviation estimate of -$7.48bn of S&P for sale over the next week.

Derivatives: VIX rose to 27.77 and VIX vol had its second-largest one-day move up ever. Hedge monetization dominated early flows in S&P, Nasdaq and VIX. NDX and SPX fixed-strike vols were bid most in the front end, and skew steepened sharply. The desk's Vol Panic Index hit 9.3 out of 10. VIX calls and call spreads were unwound as the index spiked above 26. The implied move through the next day is 1.43%.

Asia flows (Navin, HK): the day's flows were 10-15% above the 20-day average, orderly with no significant panic. The region was 1.3x better to sell, with every market net to sell, led by China, Japan and Taiwan. Sector skews: IT 1.1x better to sell, Financials 1.4x, Industrials 1.1x, Real Estate 1.2x better to buy. Most markets recovered from their opening lows except Japan.

Asia weekly flows: the desk was net to sell -$242mn, the smallest net skew of the year. Taiwan was the top net sold market for a second week (-$1.2bn), followed by Korea (-$813mn) and Singapore (-$200mn). China (+$815mn), Hong Kong (+$462mn) and India (+$371mn) were net bought. The most sold, anti-consensus markets drew the largest inflows over 10 days, with more long-only money in buy flow. The desk says it is hard to call an inflection point.

Prime book for October: large net selling, driven by long unwinds and short sales, concentrated in Asia and North America. Asian equities saw net selling with a 1-year Z-score of -0.9, long sales exceeding short sales about 5 to 1, and de-grossing at -1.0. Info Tech was the most net sold sector for a fifth straight month.

China: A-shares rebounded broadly and major indices were on track to snap six-week losing streaks. The STAR Composite rose 9.9% in one session, the largest one-day gain on record. Net inflows into 14 national-team favorite ETFs have exceeded 400bn Rmb since mid-October, far above the April 2025 intervention. Daily turnover is back above 2 trillion Rmb versus a 20-day average near 1.6 trillion. The desk's question is whether national-team support has stopped the negative feedback loop.

India: the Nifty gained 6.4% in four days, the best week since 2021, with a first close above its 200-day moving average since the late February selloff. Foreign investors bought $3.5bn in cash while domestic institutions sold $1.9bn. Turnover of $19.6bn on Thursday would rank in the year's top 3 outside rebalance days. The 10-year yield fell 30bps from about 7.5% in late October. Realty led with +10%, then Autos +8.6%, Financials +7.6% and Metals +6.9%, with no sector down.

Taiwan: the TWSE fell 8% week-to-Thursday and traded below 40,000 for the first time since April. Foreign investors have sold for 6 straight sessions totaling $19.2bn, and 19 of 20 sessions since 10/6 totaling $48bn. Local funds have bought 18 straight sessions ($11bn). Year to date foreigners are net sellers of $86.7bn including $68.9bn in TSMC. Retail margin loans fell 3.4% on Thursday to the lowest since 8/31. Reports say the regulator and the National Stabilization Fund may meet on stabilization measures. Hon Hai opened down 9.4% when much of the market opened limit down.

Korea: KOSPI closed below 5,400 on Thursday for the first time since April 3, 2026, with foreign selling of $6.8bn week-to-date, $5.8bn of it in tech. KRXSEMI fell 19.7%. Foreign selling has run 12 consecutive weeks totaling $44.1bn. Local institutions and retail bought the dip. KOSPI found support near 5,000 after a circuit breaker and sidecars, with RSI near 31 and margin loans at 0.6% of market cap.

Japan: the Nikkei fell 9.2% and TOPIX 6.6% on the week, with the Nikkei at its lowest since April and heading for the third-worst point drop ever. The desk's momentum long basket had its biggest one-day drawdown of the year. Long-only funds sold tech while hedge funds added tech and semis shorts. The short sell ratio rose to 40%. Defensives such as telcos and pharma saw safety buying. 44% of TOPIX companies reporting have beaten expectations versus 42% that missed.

tension_points.bull_case: Privorotsky leans toward a 1998-style liquidity crisis: leaders have real revenues, cash flows and balance sheets, delayed data centers do not destroy compute demand, and constrained capacity may improve existing economics. Markets recovered once liquidity returned and the Fed eased.
tension_points.bear_case: The 2000 parallel is the sheer scale of spending and uncertainty around returns, and the question is whether the economics are wrong rather than just the financing timing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Demand, utilization and returns need to hold. The view changes if evidence shows underlying spending and demand are not intact.

tension_points.bull_case: S&P sits just above its 200-day average, and Privorotsky notes the S&P has been higher 12 months after all 19 midterms since 1950.
tension_points.bear_case: Nasdaq has broken its 200-day average, futures closed below the 7,549 CTA threshold, and negative gamma leaves scope for violent moves with about $7.48bn of CTA selling estimated.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The S&P failing to hold its 200-day average, which Privorotsky says needs to hold.
